extracted.intended_audience: researchers and algorithm designers studying peer-review assignment algorithms / theoretical computer scientists working on ranking and mechanism design for peer review
extracted.subtask_description: The page analyzes algorithms that order papers shown to a reviewer (SUPER*, SIM, BID, RAND) by measuring expected paper-side and reviewer-side gains (with trade-off λ), proving worst-case additive suboptimality bounds for baselines relative to the optimal SUPER*. It provides precise model assumptions (positional discount f_π, paper gain γ_p, prior bid counts) and technical lemmas used to bound these gains.

rubrics_metrics.name: paper-side gain
rubrics_metrics.description: The component of expected gain accruing to papers (from obtaining bids); depends on similarity scores, the number of bids on each paper, and the position-dependent function f_π used to discount position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used throughout substitutions and bounds (e.g., sums of terms like (f_π(j) − f_π(j + d/2))). The paper-side gain interacts with prior bid counts through γ_p(·) differences (e.g., γ_p(g_{n−1,j}+1) − γ_p(g_{n−1,j})). The proofs rely on properties of f_π (here f_π(x)=1/log2(x+1), decreasing) to lower bound sums appearing in the paper-side gain (see Lemmas 2 and 6).

rubrics_metrics.name: reviewer-side gain
rubrics_metrics.description: The component of expected gain accruing to the reviewer for being shown similar papers; this term includes the trade-off parameter λ and depends on similarity scores and positions via f_π.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formally appears multiplied by λ in the combined objective. The reviewer-side gain is bounded analogously to the paper-side gain; manipulations use the same f_π properties to produce lower bounds (see Equations (27)–(28)).

rubrics_metrics.name: combined (total) expected gain objective
rubrics_metrics.description: The objective used to evaluate/optimize orderings: total expected gain = paper-side gain + λ × reviewer-side gain, where λ≥0 controls the trade-off.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the optimization criterion for SUPER*: weights for each paper in the optimization are α_{n,j} = S_{n,j}(γ_p(g_{n−1,j}+1) − γ_p(g_{n−1,j})) + λ(2S_{n,j} − 1). An ordering is optimal if it sorts papers in decreasing α_{n,j}; ties can be broken arbitrarily without affecting expected gain.

rubrics_metrics.name: α_{n,j} weight for per-paper ordering decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Weight assigned to paper j for the final reviewer optimization: α_{n,j} = S_{n,j}(γ_p(g_{n−1,j}+1) − γ_p(g_{n−1,j})) + λ(2S_{n,j} − 1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ranking policy SUPER* shows paper j ahead of j' if α_{n,j} > α_{n,j'}. This gives a concrete production rule: compute α and sort. The proofs use explicit α values in constructed instances to derive optimal and baseline orderings (see Sections A.3.3 and A.3.4).

rubrics_metrics.name: positional discount function f_π properties
rubrics_metrics.description: The position-dependent function f_π(x) (here f_π(x)=1/log2(x+1)) is decreasing on R_{>0} and used to weight the effect of showing a paper at earlier positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many bounds rely on monotonicity and specific bounds for f_π; e.g., Lemma 2 and Lemma 6 lower bound sums of differences f_π(j) − f_π(j + k) by expressions of order d / log2^2(d). The choice of f_π crucially affects the lower-bound constants and rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: paper-side gain function γ_p properties
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper-side gain function γ_p(x) (in the proofs γ_p(x)=√x) is increasing on R_{≥0} and used to translate bid counts into marginal paper gains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bounds use differences γ_p(1) − γ_p(0), γ_p(2) − γ_p(1), etc., to construct α_{n,j} values. Lemma 1 derives a useful lower bound on combinations of these γ_p differences under model parameter constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: suboptimality / additive worst-case gap metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure of algorithmic suboptimality: the additive difference in expected total gain between SUPER* and a baseline (SIM, BID, RAND) in the worst-case for the final reviewer, typically lower bounded by c · d / log2^2(d) for some constant c>0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorems and lemmas show existence of constants c such that for all d≥2 and λ≥0, baselines suffer an additive loss at least c·d / log2^2(d) (with explicit constant instantiations in Equations (31), (36), (42), and accompanying lemmas). This is the principal evaluation standard used to claim suboptimality.

rubrics_metrics.name: worst-case instance construction criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove lower bounds, construct adversarial problem instances where similarity scores and prior bids are arranged (e.g., half papers with S=1 and one previous bid, half with S=0 and no bids) to maximize the gap between SUPER* and a baseline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper prescribes specific constructions (Sections A.3.2–A.3.4) to exhibit failure modes of SIM, BID, and RAND. These constructions are canonical tests for evaluator algorithms: if an algorithm performs poorly on these instances it fails the robustness criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: SIM baseline failure mode
rubrics_metrics.description: SIM orders papers in decreasing similarity scores (agnostic to prior bids). This can be suboptimal because the paper-side and reviewer-side gains both depend on similarity and bid counts; SIM ignores bid counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The analysis constructs instances where showing a paper with higher similarity but fewer prior bids earlier yields significantly higher total expected gain; SIM's ordering leads to an additive gap (see Lemmas 2–3 and Equation (31)).

rubrics_metrics.name: BID baseline failure mode
rubrics_metrics.description: BID orders papers by increasing number of previous bids (greedyly optimizing minimum bid count) and is largely independent of similarity scores, which can make it suboptimal for both paper-side and reviewer-side gain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counterexamples (Section A.3.3) show instances where BID's ordering places lower-similarity papers ahead of higher-similarity ones even when gains favor the opposite, producing an additive suboptimality bound (see Equations (33)–(36) and Lemma 4 for odd d).

rubrics_metrics.name: RAND baseline failure mode
rubrics_metrics.description: RAND selects a uniform random ordering from all permutations. Because it is agnostic to both similarity and bid counts, with non-negligible probability it selects highly suboptimal orderings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Probability lemmas (Lemma 5) bound the chance RAND places too few 'good' papers early (e.g., fewer than d/4 of top-half papers in top d/2 positions with probability ≥1/6), which is used to show expected additive suboptimality of order d / log2^2(d) (see Equations (38)–(42)).

rubrics_metrics.name: tie-breaking invariance assumption
rubrics_metrics.description: Assumption used in analysis: when papers have equal α weights (or equal bids/similarity), tie-breaking by index or some fixed rule does not change the expected gain and so can be chosen w.l.o.g. for simplicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This simplifies constructions and proofs: the authors assume ties are broken in order of paper indexes (or similarly) since the tie-breaking mechanism among equal-weight sets will not impact the expected gain.

rubrics_metrics.name: probabilistic counting bounds for permutations
rubrics_metrics.description: Combinatorial/probabilistic criteria used to evaluate RAND: bounds on the number of permutations that place a given number of specified papers within specified positions (used to lower-bound probabilities of 'bad' permutations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lemma 5 gives a lower bound (≥1/6) on the probability that a random permutation places fewer than d/4 of top-half papers into the first d/2 positions. These combinatorial probabilities are used to convert permutation-level bad events into expected gain losses for RAND.
